“Very little has changed since you left, except that our dear children have grown. The blue lake and snow‑capped mountains are still the same, and I think our peaceful home and our happy hearts follow the same unchanging rules. My small chores fill my time and entertain me, and I’m rewarded for any effort by seeing only happy, kind faces around me. Since you went away, only one thing has changed in our little household. Do you remember the occasion when Justine Moritz joined our family? You probably don’t; so I’ll tell you her story briefly. Madame Moritz, her mother, was a widow with four children, and Justine was the third. She had always been her father’s favorite, but for some strange reason her mother could not stand her and, after Mr. Moritz died, treated her very poorly. My aunt saw this, and when Justine was twelve, she persuaded her mother to let her live with us. The republican institutions of our country have created simpler, happier manners than those in the great monarchies around us. There’s less distinction between the different social classes; the lower orders are neither as poor nor as despised, and their manners are more refined and moral. A servant in Geneva isn’t the same as a servant in France or England. When Justine was taken into our family, she learned the duties of a servant—a role that, in our fortunate country, does not imply ignorance or the loss of human dignity.

“Justine, you may recall, was a great favorite of yours; I remember you once said that if you were in a bad mood, a glance from Justine could lift it, just as Ariosto described Angelica’s beauty—she seemed so open‑hearted and happy. My aunt grew very attached to her, which led her to give Justine an education better than she had originally planned. That generosity was fully repaid; Justine was the most grateful little creature in the world. I don’t mean she made grand speeches—I never heard her say a word like that—but you could see in her eyes that she almost adored her protector. Though her disposition was lively and sometimes thoughtless, she paid the greatest attention to every gesture of my aunt. She saw her as the model of all excellence and tried to copy her speech and manners, so even now she often reminds me of her.

“When my dearest aunt died, everyone was so wrapped up in their own grief that they barely noticed poor Justine, who had cared for her during her illness with the deepest affection. Poor Justine was very ill herself; but other trials were still ahead for her.

“One by one, her brothers and sister died, and her mother, left with only her neglected daughter, was childless. The woman’s conscience was troubled; she began to think that the deaths of her loved ones were a heavenly judgment punishing her favoritism.”
